Taranga Jain Temple in Gujarat

Taranga, in present-day Mehsana district, Gujarat, is an important Jain pilgrimage site associated with the development of medieval western Indian temple architecture.

Its principal historic Jain temple is dedicated to Ajitanatha, the 2nd Jain Tirthankara. The major temple belongs to the 12th century CE and is traditionally attributed to Kumarapala, an important Chaulukya or Solanki ruler.

Taranga illustrates the continuation of the Maru-Gurjara tradition in the construction of substantial Jain temples. The surviving monument has also undergone later alterations and renovation, so its present form should not be assumed to represent every detail of a single original building campaign.

The site is particularly important because it combines a definite Gujarat location, a Jain dedication and a historical association with later Solanki patronage.

Palitana and the Shatrunjaya hills

Palitana, in the Saurashtra region of Gujarat, is associated with the celebrated Jain temple complex on the Shatrunjaya hills.

The site contains numerous temples and smaller shrines grouped together on a sacred hill. Their clustering demonstrates the importance of pilgrimage and repeated religious patronage.

Palitana belongs to the wider story of western Indian Jain architecture, but its temple complex developed over a long period. It should not be treated as one monument built entirely by a single Solanki ruler.

Rudra Mahalaya at Siddhpur

The architectural legacy of the Solankis also includes important Shaiva monuments. Rudra Mahalaya, also called Rudramala, is associated with Siddhpur in present-day Patan district, Gujarat.

Its major development is traditionally credited to Siddharaja Jayasimha in the 12th century. The complex was a substantial temple dedicated to Shiva, with monumental pillars, gateways and subsidiary shrines.

Only parts of the original architectural complex survive. The remaining pillars and structural fragments nevertheless indicate the scale of the original project and the capabilities of Solanki-period builders.

Rudra Mahalaya helps distinguish Solanki religious patronage from any assumption that this architecture was restricted to Sun temples or Jain temples.

The contribution of regional craftspeople

Maru-Gurjara architecture represents the work of multiple groups of craftspeople. Architects organised the spaces and structural relationships; masons shaped and assembled the stone; sculptors created sacred images, decorative panels, pillars and ceiling ornaments.

Several features distinguish their work:

  • Complex wall surfaces: alternating projections and recesses gave buildings a rhythmic exterior.
  • Elaborate halls: carved pillars and ornamental arches helped define assembly spaces.
  • Finely worked ceilings: concentric stone rings and central pendants made the interiors particularly distinctive.
  • Varied building types: similar decorative skills appeared in temples, stepwells and associated water structures.
  • Shared regional tradition: craftsmanship travelled between Gujarat and Rajasthan and served both Hindu and Jain patrons.

The development of this architecture was therefore not the achievement of a single designer, ruler or religious community. It was a regional tradition sustained by patronage, skilled workmanship and the transmission of artistic knowledge.

Distinguishing the major monuments

The most useful preliminary-examination skill is to connect each monument with its location, form, patron or historical association, and distinctive feature.

Modhera is a Sun Temple whose complex includes a large stepped kund. Rani-ki-Vav is a memorial stepwell descending below ground. Sahasralinga Talav is a large reservoir at Patan. Taranga is particularly associated with a temple of Ajitanatha. Dilwara is famous for Jain marble carving at Mount Abu in Rajasthan.

The names of individual patrons should also be kept distinct. Bhima I is associated with Modhera, while his queen Udayamati is associated with Rani-ki-Vav. Siddharaja Jayasimha is associated with Sahasralinga Talav's development and Rudra Mahalaya. Kumarapala is traditionally associated with the Jain temple at Taranga.

Prelims focus

  • Taranga: Mehsana district; Ajitanatha, the 2nd Jain Tirthankara; traditionally associated with Kumarapala.
  • Palitana: Shatrunjaya hills, Saurashtra; major Jain pilgrimage and temple complex.
  • Rudra Mahalaya: Siddhpur, Patan district; Shiva temple associated with Siddharaja Jayasimha.
  • Modhera: Bhima I, 1026–27 CE, Surya and Surya Kund.
  • Rani-ki-Vav: Udayamati, 11th century, Patan, UNESCO inscription in 2014.
  • Trap: A temple's present-day location, historical patronage and architectural style are separate facts. Do not infer one automatically from another.

[Sources: NCERT, An Introduction to Indian Art, Part I, Class 11, chapter 6, printed pp. 75–76 and 94–95; Krishna Deva, Temples of North India, 1969, chapter VI, printed pp. 45–48; Gujarat Tourism, Taranga (Hill) Jain Temple, consulted 23 November 2026; Patan District Administration, History and Tourist Places, consulted 23 November 2026; UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Rani-ki-Vav, World Heritage property 922, consulted 23 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: The Ajitanatha Jain temple at Taranga, Gujarat, showing its substantial stone construction and prominent Nagara tower.
pictures.caption: Taranga represents the Jain temple tradition associated with 12th-century Gujarat.
